title: How Much Does a Sleep Study Cost? (In-Lab vs. At-Home)
summary: How much does a sleep study cost? In-lab studies have a median hospital self-pay price near $2,961, while home sleep tests often cost under $200. See why.
body_markdown:
If you have loud snoring, wake up gasping, or feel sleepy during the day no matter how long you sleep, your doctor may recommend a sleep study. Before you book one, you probably want to know the actual cost and whether it's covered by insurance. Here's a straightforward breakdown of what an in-lab sleep study and a home sleep test cost in 2026, what drives those prices, and how to avoid surprise bills.


## Quick Answer: Typical Sleep Study Costs in 2026


- **In-lab sleep study (polysomnography):** the median hospital self-pay price is about **$2,961** , and most hospitals charge between about $1,070 and $6,370, according to[Self Pay Rates](https://selfpayrates.com/cost/sleep-study) , which compiles prices from 2,174 U.S. hospitals for CPT code 95810.
- **Home sleep test:** a survey of 15 online providers in October 2026 found a median all-in cash price of **$189** , with prices from $99 to about $465, including the doctor's review, according to[Sleep Apnea Select](https://sleepapneaselect.com/research/home-sleep-test-pricing/) .
- **With insurance:** your out-of-pocket cost depends on your deductible and coinsurance. A home sleep study usually costs much less out of pocket than an in-lab sleep study.
- **Location matters:** hospital self-pay prices vary depending on the state, from a median of about $1,198 in New Jersey to about $8,337 in Utah, according to Self Pay Rates.


## What Is a Sleep Study, and When Do You Need One?


A sleep study is a sleep test that monitors your breathing patterns, heart rate, blood oxygen level, and sometimes brain activity while you sleep. It can be done overnight in a sleep lab or as an at-home sleep study with a portable device, depending on what your clinician suspects.


Sleep studies help diagnose sleep apnea, narcolepsy, periodic limb movement disorder, restless leg syndrome, parasomnias such as sleepwalking and REM behavior disorders, and other sleep disorders.


Common reasons a doctor orders sleep apnea testing include:


- Loud snoring reported by a bed partner
- Pauses in breathing or gasping during sleep
- Morning headaches
- Excessive daytime sleepiness or trouble concentrating
- Falling asleep unintentionally, for example while driving


Sleep tests are usually ordered by a primary care clinician or a sleep specialist after an office or telehealth visit. Insurance coverage, including[Medicare](https://www.medicare.gov/coverage/sleep-studies) , generally requires signs and symptoms of a sleep disorder and a provider's order; sleep studies aren't covered as routine screening.


## Types of Sleep Tests, and Why They're Priced Differently


The more sensors, staff time, and monitoring involved, the higher the price.


**In-lab polysomnography (Type I).** You spend the night in a sleep center while a technologist monitors you. The test records brain activity, eye movements, heart rhythm, leg movements, airflow, oxygen saturation, chest motion, and body position. It's the most complete sleep test and is needed for complex sleep disorders.


**Home sleep apnea tests (Types III and IV).** You sleep in your own bed with a simpler home sleep test device. These at-home tests typically use a pulse oximeter on your finger and sensors for breathing, plus heart rate, snoring, and body position. Home tests usually don't measure brain waves or sleep stages, which is a big reason a home sleep test costs less.


**Other specialized tests:**


- **Multiple Sleep Latency Test (MSLT):** a series of daytime naps after an overnight study, used to evaluate narcolepsy
- **Maintenance of Wakefulness Test (MWT):** measures your ability to stay awake, sometimes required for safety-sensitive jobs
- **Actigraphy:** a wrist device that tracks movement over days or weeks to study sleep patterns


Insurers often send straightforward cases of suspected obstructive sleep apnea to home sleep testing first and reserve in-lab testing for more complex situations, such as serious heart or lung disease, suspected central sleep apnea, or an inconclusive home sleep study. Each sleep test has its own billing code, for example CPT 95810 for an in-lab study and 95800 or 95806 for home studies, which is why two "sleep studies" can have very different prices.


A **split-night study** combines diagnosis and treatment in just one night: the first part diagnoses sleep apnea, and the second part adjusts CPAP pressure. A split-night or separate CPAP titration study is billed under a different code (CPT 95811).


## Cost of an In-Lab Sleep Study


An in-lab sleep study is usually the most expensive option because it requires an overnight room in a sleep center, specialized equipment, and a technologist.


At hospitals, the median self-pay price for diagnostic polysomnography is about $2,961, and most hospitals charge between about $1,070 and $6,370, according to Self Pay Rates. An independent, lab-based sleep study is often less expensive than one at a hospital sleep center.


Expect two kinds of charges:


- **A technical or facility fee** for the room, sensors, monitoring, and equipment
- **A professional fee** for the sleep specialist who interprets your test results


The initial consultation and follow-up visits are billed separately. If you're uninsured or paying yourself, the No Surprises Act gives you the right to a[good faith estimate](https://www.cms.gov/initiatives/your-patient-rights/medical-bill-rights) before scheduled care.


## How Much Does a Home Sleep Test Cost?


A home sleep test usually costs far less than an in-lab study. In an October 2026 survey of 15 online providers, Sleep Apnea Select found a median price of $189, with prices from $99 to about $465, for home sleep tests that included the doctor's review, required visits, and standard shipping.


Not every home sleep test cost is comparable. Some providers sell only the device rental, while others bundle a telehealth visit before the test, interpretation by a sleep specialist, and a follow-up visit to discuss treatment options. Check what's included before comparing.


Because a home sleep apnea test collects less data than an in-lab study, it's typically used for adults with a high likelihood of uncomplicated obstructive sleep apnea. If the device doesn't capture enough data or the results are unclear, you may need an in-lab study, which adds cost.


## With Insurance: Deductibles, Coinsurance, and Out-of-Pocket Cost


What most people care about is not the billed price but the out-of-pocket cost after insurance.


**Commercial insurance plans:**


- Sleep studies are diagnostic tests, so they usually count toward your[deductible](https://www.withflex.com/blog/what-is-a-deductible) .
- After you meet your deductible, you typically pay[coinsurance](https://www.withflex.com/blog/what-is-coinsurance) , plus any[copays](https://www.withflex.com/blog/what-is-a-copay) for office or telehealth visits.
- Prior authorization is often required, especially for in-lab studies.


**Medicare:** Medicare Part B covers Type I, II, III, and IV sleep tests if you have clinical signs and symptoms of sleep apnea. After you meet the Part B deductible, you pay 20% of the Medicare-approved amount. Medicare covers Type I tests only when they're done in a sleep lab facility, according to Medicare.gov.


**Expect several bills:**


- The initial office or telehealth visit
- The sleep test itself
- The specialist's interpretation and follow-up visit
- Equipment such as a CPAP machine, if you're diagnosed with sleep apnea


Someone who has already met their deductible may owe only coinsurance. Someone early in the year on a high-deductible insurance plan may owe the full negotiated price until the deductible is met.


Before scheduling, call your insurance company with the procedure code (CPT 95810 or 95811 for in-lab studies, 95800 or 95806 for home tests) and the sleep center's information, and ask for an estimate. Make sure the sleep center is[in-network](https://www.withflex.com/blog/in-network-vs-out-of-network) .


## Paying Without Insurance


If you're paying out of pocket, ask for the self-pay price. Many sleep centers and home testing companies offer discounted cash prices, and a home sleep test is usually the least expensive option when it's medically appropriate.


Compare at least two options. In the same area, one sleep lab may quote a much higher self-pay price than another, or offer a bundled package that includes the study and interpretation.


Common payment options include in-house payment plans and discounts for paying in full. Also ask about:


- Missed appointment or late cancellation fees for in-lab studies
- Shipping and return fees for home tests
- Charges for repeating a test if the first night's data can't be used


Whether you can pay with an HSA or FSA depends on your plan's rules, and[IRS Publication 502](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p502) describes which medical expenses qualify. Our guide to[HSAs and FSAs](https://www.withflex.com/blog/what-are-hsas-fsas) explains how the two accounts work.


## Important Factors That Drive the Price of a Sleep Study


- **Type of test:** in-lab polysomnography, a home sleep apnea test, or a specialized test such as the MSLT
- **CPAP titration:** whether it happens the same night (split-night) or in a second study
- **Facility type:** hospital sleep centers often charge more than independent labs or home testing companies
- **Location:** prices vary widely by state and city
- **Your insurance provider's contract:** the negotiated rate your plan allows determines your deductible and coinsurance amounts
- **Professional fees:** interpretation, scoring, and follow-up visits can be billed separately
- **Repeat testing:** a second study after starting treatment adds cost


## Home vs. In-Lab Sleep Studies: Cost and Comfort Tradeoffs


**Home sleep tests:**


- Cost much less
- Let you sleep in your own bed
- Measure breathing, blood oxygen, heart rate, and body position, but usually not brain activity or sleep stages
- Work well for adults with suspected moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea and no other major health problems


**In-lab sleep studies:**


- Use more sensors, including brain activity monitoring, with a technologist watching overnight, which tends to give more accurate results in one night
- Are preferred for narcolepsy, parasomnias, suspected central sleep apnea, periodic limb movement disorder, and unexplained sleep issues


At-home tests can underestimate milder sleep apnea or miss other sleep disorders. If a home test is inconclusive, you may need an in-lab study, which adds cost and time. Talk with your clinician about which sleep test fits your symptoms and budget.


## What Happens After the Sleep Study, and What Sleep Apnea Treatment Costs


After your test, a technologist scores the data and a sleep specialist interprets it. You'll then have a follow-up visit to go over your test results, including your apnea-hypopnea index (the number of breathing pauses per hour), and agree on a treatment plan.


Common follow-up costs include:


- A follow-up visit to discuss results and treatment options
- A CPAP or BiPAP machine and supplies if you're diagnosed with obstructive sleep apnea
- An oral appliance if CPAP isn't a good fit


Each of these has its own billing code and cost-sharing. Sleep apnea treatment matters for your sleep health and overall health: untreated sleep apnea is a serious condition that increases the risk of stroke, heart attack, and other serious problems, according to the[National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/sleep-apnea) .


## How to Get an Accurate Cost Estimate Before You Book


1. Ask your clinician which sleep test they recommend, in-lab or home, and why.
2. Ask for the procedure codes for the test and any related visits.
3. Call the sleep center and your insurance provider. Confirm whether prior authorization is needed, the allowed amount under your plan, and how much you've already paid toward your deductible and out-of-pocket maximum.


Also ask about separate interpretation fees, follow-up visit charges, repeat-test fees, and cancellation policies.


If it's medically appropriate, compare at least one in-lab sleep center and one home sleep testing service. Get the numbers in writing before your study night so you can focus on getting a diagnosis and starting treatment.
